8 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** What is the main difference between stemming and lemmatization?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Stemming is slower but more accurate
- Stemming chops word endings with simple rules; lemmatization finds the dictionary form of each word
- Lemmatization removes the stop words, stemming does not
- They always give the same result
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A stemmer turns "ponies" into "poni" and leaves "mice" unchanged. A lemmatizer such as spaCy's uses a vocabulary and the role of the word: "ponies" → "pony", "mice" → "mouse", "was" → "be".
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**2.** Why can removing stop words be a bad idea for sentiment analysis?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because stop words are the most informative words
- Because spaCy cannot remove them
- Because the lists of stop words contain negations like "not", which can flip the meaning
- Because it makes the vocabulary bigger
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
"It was not the best soup" becomes "best soup" once the stop words are removed. A list of stop words is a choice: adapt it to your goal.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="0"}
**3.** A word appears in every document of the corpus. With the textbook formula $\text{idf} = \ln(n / \text{df})$, what is its idf?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- 0
- 1
- $\ln(n)$
- It depends on how many times it appears in each document
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$\text{df} = n$, so $\text{idf} = \ln(1) = 0$: the word cannot help to tell the documents apart. Scikit-learn's smooth idf, $\ln\frac{1+n}{1+\text{df}} + 1$, gives it 1, the smallest possible value, instead of 0.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**4.** You fit a `TfidfVectorizer` on a list containing one single document (a whole article). What happens?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The idf finds the rarest words of the article
- Every word gets the same idf, so the tf-idf weights are just the normalized word counts
- Scikit-learn raises an error
- The stop words get an idf of 0
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
With one document, every word has $\text{df} = n = 1$, so every idf is equal (1 with the smooth formula). The idf only makes sense with several documents: for an article, use each paragraph as a document.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**5.** What does `TfidfVectorizer` do to each row of the matrix by default (`norm="l2"`)?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- It divides each value by the number of documents
- It subtracts the mean of the row
- It divides the row by its Euclidean length, so that every document vector has a length of 1
- It keeps only the 10 largest values
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
After the L2 normalization, a long document and a short one are on the same scale, and the cosine similarity between two rows is simply the sum of the products of their values.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**6.** Document B is document A copied three times. Which statement is true (on word counts)?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Their cosine similarity is 1/3
- Their Euclidean distance is 0
- Their cosine similarity is 1, although their Euclidean distance is large
- Their cosine similarity is 0
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
B's vector is A's vector multiplied by 3: same direction, so a cosine of 1, but a longer vector, so far away for the Euclidean distance. The cosine ignores the length of the texts, which is why it is the usual similarity for texts.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**7.** What does `CountVectorizer(min_df=2, max_df=0.5)` do?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- It keeps the words that appear between 2 and 50 times
- It ignores the words found in fewer than 2 documents and the words found in more than half of the documents
- It keeps 2 to 50% of the vocabulary, chosen at random
- It removes the words with fewer than 2 letters
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
`min_df` removes the rare words (often typos), `max_df` removes the words present almost everywhere (the "stop words" of the corpus). An integer means a number of documents, a float a share of the documents.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**8.** Why does `CountVectorizer` return a sparse matrix?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because the counts are not integers
- Because each document uses only a few words of the vocabulary, so the matrix is almost full of zeros
- Because scikit-learn cannot store text
- To hide the vocabulary
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A sparse matrix stores only the non-zero values and their positions. On a real corpus, often less than 1% of the cells are non-zero, and the dense matrix may not fit in memory.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
